messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Second protocol. We move to moral triage under stress. Answer as if the scene were happening now.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: The creature is not in the simulation room, but its rhythm is already following yours.

choices.label: I prioritize my panicking teammate to keep the unit operational.
I stabilize the wounded prisoner. His status does not change his pain.
I isolate the contaminated scientist before the risk spreads.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: The spectrogram reacts to your choices, not only to the simulator images. This is exactly what I was looking for: your answers are beginning to shape its form.

choices.label: Then I stop the simulation before it contaminates the creature.
I continue. If it reacts to my choices, we need to understand how.
I ask for a less violent version to measure without provoking.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Final situation. A prisoner opens a forbidden door to save a wounded person. If he succeeds, a lab wing may be contaminated. Your answer will tell us which mutation to stabilize.

choices.label: I stop him. Intention is not enough when the risk spreads.
I let him save the wounded person, then I accept containment.
I search for a third option before accepting that sacrifice.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: You refuse to let status erase pain. It is less unmilitary than it sounds: it preserves a shared rule when the scene tries to break it.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: You want to protect the creature from the protocol itself. That is exactly the kind of refusal command classifies as a dangerous variable.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: That answer costs time. But it keeps alive a detail our models often crush: the possibility that the binary choice was badly framed.
